title: Species of different genera and classes change at different rates

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species of different genera and classes change at different rates

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species of different genera and classes have not changed at the same rate or to the same degree through geological time.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Species of different genera and classes have not changed at the same rate, or in the same degree.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter X, “On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings”; section “On their different rates of change”. Scope: fossil and living species across taxonomic groups

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch10-02: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.80

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Heterogeneous evolutionary rates are directly measurable with established comparative methods and public matrices. Full cross-life comparability is limited, but the general claim is readily exposed to refutation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate lineage-specific morphological or molecular evolutionary rates and net character change across genera and classes. Test whether among-group rate variance exceeds measurement and sampling error and whether accumulated change differs among groups.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Comparable characters are scarce across classes.

Taxonomic duration and preservation can inflate rate differences.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Unequal rates are a direct, confirm-or-refute contrast, and class-level marine turnover is downloadable and analyzable with ordinary subsampling. Taxonomic practice can inflate differences, but that bias is measurable by comparing sampling-standardized rates. Morphological rates add a check for a subset of clades and are not required for the taxonomic reading of the claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate taxonomic turnover, or morphological rate where character data exist, separately by class and by genus, and test whether those rates are equal. A wide spread of rates would support the claim; statistically indistinguishable rates across classes would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Classes differ in preservation and in how finely taxonomists split them, which can imitate rate differences.

Direct morphological rates exist for far fewer groups than taxonomic turnover does.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If different classes and genera change at different rates, then taxonomic turnover measured as the stratigraphic duration of extinct genera in the Paleobiology Database should differ substantially among major animal classes, and, within classes, among orders.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: For each of 14 higher taxa the PBDB genus list with appearance ages was downloaded; accepted extinct genera with >= 5 occurrences were kept and duration computed as the difference between first- and last-appearance midpoints. Clause A: Kruskal-Wallis across higher taxa with epsilon-squared effect size and the ratio of extreme group medians. Clause B: within each higher taxon with >= 3 orders of >= 20 genera, Kruskal-Wallis across orders. The whole procedure was repeated with >= 20 occurrences as a sensitivity check.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Using PBDB genus-rank taxa with first- and last-appearance ages for 14 higher taxa (Trilobita, Brachiopoda, Bivalvia, Gastropoda, Cephalopoda, Anthozoa, Echinoidea, Crinoidea, Ostracoda, Bryozoa, Mammalia, Reptilia, Actinopterygii, Chondrichthyes), restricted to extinct genera with >= 5 occurrences, genus duration = midpoint of first-appearance range minus midpoint of last-appearance range. Clause A (between classes): a Kruskal-Wallis test of genus duration across the higher taxa has p < 0.001 AND epsilon-squared effect size >= 0.02 AND the ratio of the largest to the smallest group median duration is >= 2. Clause B (between genera grouped by order, within classes): within each higher taxon having >= 3 orders with >= 20 qualifying genera each, a Kruskal-Wallis test of genus duration across orders has p < 0.001 and epsilon-squared >= 0.02; clause B passes if this holds in a majority of eligible higher taxa. Verdict 'supports' if A and B pass; 'mixed' if exactly one passes; 'refutes' if neither.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Clause A fails if genus durations are statistically indistinguishable across classes (p >= 0.001), or the effect is trivial (epsilon-squared < 0.02), or every class median lies within a factor of 2 of every other. Clause B fails if orders within a class differ significantly and non-trivially in half or fewer of the eligible classes. Both failing refutes the claim. A sensitivity re-run with >= 20 occurrences per genus is reported; if the sign of either clause flips under that filter the result is downgraded to 'mixed' regardless.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: ratio of largest to smallest median genus duration among the 14 higher taxa (Myr/Myr)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'rate of change' of species is read, following the Grok assessor, as taxonomic turnover: shorter genus durations mean faster replacement of forms. 'Classes' are mapped to PBDB classes or, where PBDB class structure is unstable (brachiopods, bryozoans), phyla. 'Species of different genera' is approximated by genera grouped into orders, because species-level ranges in PBDB are too noisy and species durations are strongly tied to the genus concept. Durations are taxonomic, not morphological; the morphological reading (rates of character change) is not tested. Differences in preservation potential and taxonomic splitting between classes can mimic rate differences, which is why the pass criterion requires a non-trivial effect size and a two-fold spread of medians rather than mere significance.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Paleobiology Database taxa lists (genus rank, show=app,class) for 14 higher taxa

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Genus duration is a taxonomic proxy for rate of change; it conflates true evolutionary rate with preservation potential, sampling intensity and how finely each class is split by taxonomists.

Durations of genera with few occurrences are truncated; the >= 5 occurrence filter (and the >= 20 sensitivity run) reduces but does not remove range truncation, which differs among classes.

Groups are not all of class rank (Brachiopoda and Bryozoa are phyla) because PBDB class membership is unstable for them.

Only extinct genera are included (extant genera have open-ended durations), which excludes the long-lived 'living fossil' lineages Darwin also had in mind and so is conservative with respect to the spread of rates.

Darwin's phrase covers rate 'or degree' of change; morphological degree of change is not measured here.
